What the official sources say

  • Local real estate assessors must assess at 100 percent fair market value in localities with annual assessments. (Va. Code 58.1-3201; source)
  • Local board of equalization hears complaints and may increase or decrease assessments; assessor's valuation is presumed correct. (Va. Code 58.1-3379; source)
  • Market sales through December 31 before the assessment's effective date may be considered if submitted by the locality's application deadline. (Va. Code 58.1-3379; source)
  • In circuit court proceedings, the taxpayer burden of proof applies except in proceedings seeking relief from real property taxes. (Va. Code 58.1-3984; source)

Who sets and collects property tax in Virginia?

Virginia real estate tax is local. The state does not bill a house; your county, city or town does, and rates, due dates and many relief programs vary by locality. Virginia is divided into 95 counties and 38 independent cities, which the Census Bureau treats as county equivalents, and the differences between a county and a city are small and relate to how each assesses new taxes, bond referendums and Dillon's Rule (Wikipedia, Virginia).

Two local officers matter most. The commissioner of the revenue, or an equivalent assessing officer, sets the value and handles corrections. The treasurer, or an equivalent officer, collects the bill and runs delinquent tax enforcement. Both offices are listed on your locality's website, and the treasurer can give you a payoff figure for a closing.

How is a Virginia house valued for tax?

All real estate is taxable unless the law exempts it, and general reassessments and annual assessments are made at 100 percent of fair market value (Va. Code 58.1-3201). A tax bill therefore tracks the locality's estimate of what the house would sell for, not what you paid.

How often that estimate changes depends on where you live. Counties must reassess every four years, or every three if the board of supervisors votes for it. A county with a population of 50,000 or less may choose five or six year intervals, and Augusta and Bedford counties have the same option (Va. Code 58.1-3252). A county or city with a qualified full-time appraiser may instead adopt biennial or annual assessment by ordinance, in which case real estate is assessed as of January 1 each year (Va. Code 58.1-3253).

Assessment methodFrequencyStatute
County general reassessmentEvery four years, or three by board vote58.1-3252
Small county (50,000 or fewer people)May elect five or six years58.1-3252
County or city with a qualified appraiserBiennial or annual by ordinance58.1-3253

When is Virginia property tax due, and what are the penalties?

Each locality sets its own due dates. A governing body may require payment in a single installment or in two equal installments, and it sets penalties and interest by ordinance (Va. Code 58.1-3916). Check the treasurer's calendar for your address, because two neighboring localities can bill on different schedules.

The state caps what a locality can add. Interest may start the day after the due date at no more than 10 percent a year, with a higher ceiling for the second and later years of delinquency. A late payment penalty cannot exceed 10 percent of the tax past due, or $10 if that is greater, and never more than the tax itself. A locality may also recover collection or attorney fees actually contracted for, up to 20 percent of the delinquent taxes.

Some relief exists in the same statute:

  • A locality may grant a payment extension of up to 90 days for good cause.
  • Members of the armed forces deployed outside the United States get an automatic extension on real estate tax on a primary residence, ending 90 days after deployment.
  • No penalty applies when a late assessment was the fault of a local official and is paid within two weeks of the notice.

How do I appeal a Virginia property assessment?

Start with the assessor's office, then the local board of equalization, then the circuit court. The board hears complaints, can raise as well as lower assessments, and works from a presumption that the assessor's value is correct. To win, the owner must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the property is valued above fair market value, or that the assessment is not uniform and was not done under accepted appraisal practice (Va. Code 58.1-3379).

Market sales through December 31 before the assessment's effective date can be used, if the owner submits them by the locality's application deadline. For a home with fewer than four residential units, the assessor must provide written notice and, on written request, the assessment records within 15 days.

Two other paths exist:

  • Application to the commissioner of the revenue for correction, within three years of the end of the tax year or one year from assessment, whichever is later. For real estate, this reaches errors made by the commissioner or factual errors in a general reassessment (Va. Code 58.1-3980).
  • Application to the circuit court, within three years from the last day of the tax year, or one year from assessment or the final determination of an earlier step, whichever is later. For real estate, the court starts from the same presumption that the assessor's value is correct (Va. Code 58.1-3984).

A bill is not treated as delinquent while an administrative appeal is pending, as long as the appeal was filed within 90 days of the assessment, and for 30 days after the final decision.

Are there exemptions or deferrals for older owners?

Possibly, but only if your locality has adopted them. A county, city or town may by ordinance exempt or defer real estate tax for owners who are at least 65, or permanently and totally disabled if the ordinance says so, and who occupy the property as their sole dwelling (Va. Code 58.1-3210).

The ordinance can limit relief to the increase in tax since the owner reached 65 or became disabled. A home held by a life estate, a revocable trust the owner controls, or certain irrevocable trusts can qualify, but a leasehold interest cannot. Ask your commissioner of the revenue about income and net worth limits, because those are set locally and differ from place to place.

What happens to unpaid property tax when a Virginia house sells?

The tax has to be paid from the sale. Real estate taxes are a lien ahead of every other lien until the taxing authority is actually paid, and the buyer, or the trustee at a foreclosure sale, must see that proceeds go to taxes and levies assessed on the property (Va. Code 58.1-3340). Taxes and levies there include accrued penalty and interest. The lien also reaches rents for the current year.

For a partial sale of a larger tract, the proration follows the purchase price in relation to the assessed value of the whole tract. The seller's liability is prorated in the contract.

Timing at the closing table adds a wrinkle. If ownership changes after January 1 and the bill has already gone out, the treasurer may cancel the bill sent to the prior owner and reissue it to the new owner, and no penalty applies if the new bill is paid within two weeks of notice.

What if the taxes are years behind?

The locality can sue to sell the property. Real estate with taxes delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the due date can be sold, and the clock is one year for property with a condemned structure, a nuisance, a derelict building or a blighted designation. Property assessed at $100,000 or less can be sold on a court finding of delinquency after the first anniversary (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Before suing, the collecting officer must send notice at least 30 days ahead to the owner's address on file and to the property address, and publish the list in a local newspaper. The owner can redeem any time before the sale by paying everything owed. Partial payment does not stop the case. The treasurer may suspend the sale under an installment agreement of up to 72 months, which must also keep current taxes paid.

If a property is sold, the former owner and heirs are entitled to the surplus after taxes, penalties, interest, fees, costs and liens, but must claim it within two years of confirmation or it goes to the locality (Va. Code 58.1-3967).

What do taxes mean for a quick sale of a Virginia house?

They mean the payoff figure matters more than the headline price. Before agreeing to any offer, request a current tax statement from the treasurer and ask the title company to list every lien. Add the state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100 and the seller's grantor tax of 50 cents per $500, unless the contract shifts it (Va. Code 58.1-802).

Owners with a pending assessment appeal, a deferral under a local ordinance or an installment agreement should tell the buyer's title company early, since each of these can affect what is owed at closing.

More questions about Virginia Property Tax Guide

Who do I call about my Virginia property tax bill?

Your locality's treasurer collects the bill, and the commissioner of the revenue or equivalent assessing office sets the value. Both are county, city or town offices, not state offices.

How often is my house reassessed?

In a county, at least every four years, or three if the board of supervisors votes for it, with five or six year options for counties of 50,000 people or fewer. A county or city with a qualified appraiser may assess annually or every two years.

What is the highest penalty a locality may charge for late real estate tax?

A penalty may not exceed 10 percent of the tax past due, or $10 if greater, and never more than the tax itself. Interest may not exceed 10 percent a year, with a higher ceiling in the second and later years.

Can I sell a house while a tax appeal is open?

Yes. The unpaid tax is still a lien, so expect the title company to pay it from proceeds. Tell them about the appeal so the payoff is figured correctly.

Does Virginia have a senior property tax break?

Only where the locality has adopted one. A county, city or town may exempt or defer tax for owners age 65 or older, or disabled if the ordinance allows, on a sole dwelling.

How long do I have to pay before a house can be sold for taxes?

Delinquency on December 31 after the second anniversary of the due date is the usual trigger. It is one year for condemned, nuisance, derelict or blighted property, and for property assessed at $100,000 or less on a court finding.

What the official sources say

  • Localities may by ordinance exempt or defer real estate taxes for owner-occupied sole dwellings of persons at least 65 or, if the ordinance provides, permanently and totally disabled. (Va. Code 58.1-3210; source)
  • Real property of a veteran rated 100 percent service-connected, permanent and total disabled, occupied as principal residence, is exempt from real property tax (tax years from 2011). (Va. Code 58.1-3219.5; source)
  • Surviving spouse of an eligible veteran qualifies so long as the spouse does not remarry. (Va. Code 58.1-3219.5; source)
  • Creditor-process homestead exemption: $5,000 ($10,000 if age 65+), plus up to $50,000 in value for principal residence of householder or dependents, plus $500 per dependent. (Va. Code 34-4; source)

What does the Virginia homestead exemption protect?

Virginia's homestead exemption shields a householder's property from creditor process on a debt, up to dollar limits set in Va. Code 34-4. It is a debt-collection protection, and it is separate from the property tax relief programs that carry a similar name in conversation.

The statute gives every householder a choice of real and personal property to hold exempt, including money and debts owed to them. Part of the amount can be used on anything. A second layer applies only to property used as the principal residence of the householder or the householder's dependents.

Piece of the exemptionAmount in the statute
General exemption, any property you pick$5,000
General exemption if the householder is 65 or older$10,000
Principal residence of the householder or dependentsUp to $50,000 in value
Each dependent, when support is shownUp to $500
Veteran with a service-connected disability rated 40 percent or more (34-4.1)Additional $10,000

A dependent is someone who gets most support from the householder and does not have enough assets to support themselves, and no one can be a dependent of more than one householder.

Will the dollar limits change?

Yes. The statute calls for an inflation adjustment on April 1, 2027, and every three years after that, using the change in the CPI-U over the most recent three-year period, rounded to the nearest $25.

Adjustments do not apply to bankruptcy cases begun before April 1, 2027. Because the amounts in your case depend on the filing date, check the current text of 34-4 on the Virginia legislature site before relying on a number from any summary, including this one.

How do you claim the exemption on real estate?

You claim it by signing a homestead deed, having it acknowledged and recording it like any other deed. The rules are in Va. Code 34-6, and nothing in the statute says it happens automatically.

  • The deed is recorded in the county or city where the real estate sits, or if the property is outside Virginia, where the householder lives in the Commonwealth.
  • It must declare the intention to claim the benefit and describe the property with reasonable certainty, with the householder's cash valuation.
  • The statute supplies a form that asks for the householder's name, dependents' names and ages, whether the veteran add-on is claimed, and any earlier homestead deeds.
  • In a federal bankruptcy case, the filed schedule of property claimed as exempt is enough to set property apart.

Personal property works the same way under 34-14, except the writing is recorded where the householder lives. The exemption can be set apart any time before the property is sold under creditor process or by a bankruptcy trustee. For garnished wages, the claim can be filed after the summons is served on the employer and on or before the return date.

Which debts can defeat a homestead claim?

Two categories are barred by 34-5: the purchase price of the property, and spousal or child support. The exemption also gives way to a waiver. Under 34-22, a person who writes a waiver on a bond, note or other instrument can have exempt property reached for that debt.

The wording that works is short: a statement that the signer waives the benefit of the exemption as to that obligation. A lender, in other words, may already have asked you to give up the protection when you borrowed.

Where a creditor has a mortgage, deed of trust or other lien on the property, the lien can be enforced first without exhausting other assets. The homestead also yields to that kind of secured claim, because the real estate was set apart subject to paramount encumbrances.

What happens to the exemption when you sell the house?

You may sell a homestead like any other real estate, and the buyer does not have to check how you use the money. Section 34-9 says exempt real estate can be sold, conveyed or exchanged, and the purchaser is not bound to see to the application of the purchase money.

  • If you reinvest the proceeds, the new property is exempt to the same extent as the old (34-20).
  • Property bought in an exchange or without a court order needs its own recorded writing, which must state where the funds came from.
  • Rents and profits from exempt property are exempt in the same manner (34-18).
  • If you stop being a householder or leave Virginia, the right to claim the exemption ends (34-24).
  • Amounts you set apart count against your maximum for eight years (34-21).

One more detail from 34-13: the part of the exemption tied to a principal residence can only be used on that kind of property and its proceeds, not on other assets. A creditor can also ask a court to reach any value over the limit if the property was worth more than the exemption when you set it apart (34-19).

How is this different from property tax relief?

Property tax relief lowers or defers the local real estate tax bill, and the rules come from a different part of the Code. The two most common programs are local and veteran based.

  • Under 58.1-3210, a locality may by ordinance exempt or defer real estate tax for a home that is the sole dwelling of an owner who is at least 65 or, if the ordinance says so, permanently and totally disabled.
  • The ordinance may limit the break to the increase in tax since the year the owner turned 65 or became disabled, or since the ordinance began, whichever is later.
  • Under 58.1-3219.5, a veteran rated 100 percent service-connected and permanently and totally disabled is exempt on a principal residence, plus up to one acre of land, for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2011.
  • A surviving spouse keeps that exemption until remarriage and can move to a new residence without losing it.

Because the elderly and disabled program is a local choice, the age, income and net worth rules are set by your city or county. We did not confirm any single locality's ordinance from an official page, so ask the commissioner of the revenue or the treasurer for current terms and filing dates.

Does the homestead exemption matter if you want to sell fast?

It can, when an owner is behind on bills and judgment creditors might reach the house. A homestead deed sets a floor of protected value, and any value above that can still be pursued, so the sale price and the liens on the title matter more than the exemption alone.

If you are weighing a quick sale, we can talk through your situation. For the legal side, an attorney who does debtor-creditor work in Virginia can tell you whether a homestead deed is worth recording before closing.

More questions about Virginia Homestead Exemption

How much is the Virginia homestead exemption?

Under 34-4, a householder can protect $5,000 of chosen property ($10,000 at age 65 or older), plus up to $50,000 of value in a principal residence, plus up to $500 per dependent. Those amounts are set to be adjusted for inflation beginning April 1, 2027.

Do you have to file a homestead deed in Virginia?

Yes for real estate. You sign a writing, have it acknowledged and record it in the county or city where the property is located. In a bankruptcy case, the filed schedule of exemptions can serve as the setting-apart document.

Does the exemption protect against child support or a purchase money loan?

No. Section 34-5 bars the exemption against the purchase price of the property and against spousal or child support obligations.

Can you sell a house after setting it apart as a homestead?

Yes. Exempt real estate can be sold and the buyer need not watch how you apply the money. Proceeds you reinvest stay exempt to the same extent if the new property is documented properly.

Is the homestead exemption the same as the senior property tax break?

No. The homestead exemption protects property from creditors. The senior and disabled tax relief in 58.1-3210 is a local program that lowers or defers real estate tax, and each locality sets its own terms.

Does a veteran get any extra protection?

A veteran with a service-connected disability rated 40 percent or more gets an additional $10,000 creditor exemption under 34-4.1. A veteran rated 100 percent permanent and total can also qualify for the real property tax exemption in 58.1-3219.5.

Virginia Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

What the official sources say

Does Virginia have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

No. Virginia Tax states that the Commonwealth no longer has an estate tax or an inheritance tax, so an heir does not owe a state death tax just for receiving a house.

The history explains why older advice still circulates. Before July 1, 2007, Virginia had an estate tax equal to the federal credit for state death taxes. When the federal credit was eliminated, the Virginia tax was effectively repealed with it.

One narrow exception remains. Virginia Tax says certain remainder interests are still subject to the inheritance tax and points readers to the estate and inheritance section of Public Document 15-93. If the house passes through a life estate or a trust with a remainder, ask a probate attorney or the department before you assume the answer is zero.

Probate tax rate10 cents per $100 of estate valueCode 58.1-1712

What is the Virginia probate tax, and is it the same as an estate tax?

It is a different charge. The probate tax is imposed when a will is probated or an administrator is appointed, and it is based on the value of the estate rather than on who inherits.

Under Code 58.1-1712 the rate is 10 cents for every $100 of value, or fraction of $100. The statute says it does not apply to decedents' estates of $15,000 or less. As a rough check on the arithmetic, the statute's rate works out to $100 of tax on a $100,000 estate, and the statute says value is determined under the next section, 58.1-1713.

For current steps and any filing fees, ask the circuit court clerk in the city or county where the person lived.

Who has the power to sell an inherited house in Virginia?

When the will tells the executor to sell the real estate, the executor has the power to sell and convey it and to receive the proceeds, provided no one else was named to sell. Code 64.2-521 says so directly.

If no executor qualifies, or those who qualified die, resign, or are removed, an administrator with the will annexed holds that same power unless the will clearly says otherwise.

  • Locate the will and the certificate showing who is the personal representative.
  • Read the will for any direction to sell the real estate.
  • Collect the deed, the latest tax bill, and any mortgage statement.
  • Ask the title company what it needs from the clerk's office before closing.

No Virginia estate tax payment is part of that list. Ask the title company what authority papers it wants to see.

What tax bills attach to an inherited house even without an estate tax?

Real estate tax stays attached to the house after a death, and it has a priority that surprises many heirs. Code 58.1-3340 puts the lien for real estate tax ahead of every other lien or encumbrance, and it stays until the taxing authority is actually paid.

Penalties and interest count as taxes under that section, and the purchaser at a sale must see that proceeds go to taxes and levies on the real estate. The seller's share is prorated by contract, so the purchase agreement should say who covers which dates.

Local rules vary by city and county. In Virginia Beach, for example, installments are due December 5 and June 5, late payments carry a 10% penalty or $10, whichever is greater, plus interest at 9.6% a year, and a lien can be recorded with the Circuit Court clerk if taxes stay unpaid. Once taxes are three years plus the current tax year delinquent, the Treasurer may advertise the property and charges a $25 fee.

An heir who has inherited a house with tax behind on it should ask the local Treasurer for a payoff figure before listing, since the title company will pay it from proceeds.

What does the deed cost when heirs sell?

The sale deed carries the same grantor tax as any other Virginia sale. Code 58.1-802 sets it at 50 cents for each $500 of consideration or fraction of it, paid by the grantor unless the parties agree the grantee will pay some or all.

The clerk will not record a deed unless the consideration is stated on its first page and the clerk has certified that the tax was paid. The tax is collected through the clerk and shared between the state and the locality.

Whether the estate or the buyer bears it follows the contract.

What about the federal side of an inherited sale?

Federal income tax can still apply to gain, even though Virginia has no estate tax. The IRS says that if you received an asset by inheritance, your basis is figured under special rules found in Publication 551, Basis of Assets, not by the usual cost rule.

The IRS also says that property acquired from a decedent has its own holding-period exceptions, which are covered in Publication 544. Whether a gain exists at all depends on the basis and the sale price.

  • Ask the estate's tax preparer how basis was set for the house.
  • Remember that the $250,000 and $500,000 home sale exclusion requires you to have owned and used the home as your main residence for 24 months out of the last 5 years.
  • If you receive Form 1099-S, report the sale even when the gain is excludable.
  • A loss on a personal-use home is not deductible, according to the IRS.

A separate page on this site explains how the federal rules interact with Virginia income tax on a house sale.

When does an as-is cash sale help an estate?

It helps when the family wants a closing date, not repairs, and when carrying costs are rising. Real estate tax, insurance, utilities, and yard care continue for as long as the estate holds the house, and a vacant house adds its own risks.

An as-is sale avoids repair negotiations, which can matter when heirs live in different states. Title and closing still go through a title company, and the personal representative must have authority to convey.

We can walk through the paperwork with you and answer questions about timing. We are not tax or legal advisors, and a probate attorney should confirm who may sign.

More questions about Virginia Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Virginia charge an inheritance tax on a house I inherit?

No. Virginia Tax says the state no longer has an inheritance tax, with a narrow exception for certain remainder interests. Ask a probate attorney if the house came through a life estate or trust remainder.

What is the Virginia probate tax rate?

The probate tax is 10 cents for every $100 of estate value under Code 58.1-1712, and it does not apply to estates of $15,000 or less.

Can an executor sell the house without all heirs signing?

If the will devises the real estate to be sold and names no one else to sell it, the executor has the power to sell and convey under Code 64.2-521. Other situations depend on the will, so confirm with an attorney.

Who pays the real estate tax owed on an inherited house at closing?

It is paid from the sale proceeds. The tax lien has priority over other liens under Code 58.1-3340, and the contract prorates the seller's share.

Do I owe federal tax when I sell an inherited house?

Possibly. Federal income tax applies to gain, and the IRS says inherited property has its own basis rules in Publication 551. Many sales produce little or no gain, but confirm with a tax professional.

Where can I read the official rule on remainder interests?

Virginia Tax points to the Virginia Estate and Inheritance Taxes section of Public Document 15-93 on its estate and inheritance tax page.

What the official sources say

  • If a dwelling is foreclosed and a tenant is in occupancy, a successor acquiring for primary residence must give notice to vacate at least 90 days out. (Va. Code Title 55.1 Ch. 12 (VRLTA), foreclosure successor provision; source)
  • A successor acquiring for any other purpose takes subject to the rental agreement and tenant may occupy for the remaining lease term, subject to termination under 55.1-1245. (VRLTA (foreclosure successor provision); source)
  • Residential executory contracts (installment, lease-option, rent-to-own) are subject to the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. (Va. Code 55.1-3002; source)

How does a Virginia eviction case begin in court?

A Virginia landlord starts an eviction by asking a magistrate, a court clerk or a general district court judge for a summons, backed by a sworn statement of the facts that justify removing the tenant. The case is called an unlawful detainer, and it is filed under Va. Code 8.01-126.

For a residential tenancy, the first hearing is supposed to come as soon as practicable and no more than 21 days after filing. If the court cannot fit the case in by then, the hearing must still happen within 30 days of filing. The summons has to be served at least 10 days before the return date. A landlord can ask for a later first date, and the court will pick one that works for both the plaintiff and the court.

The statute also sets a floor on paperwork. The court may not enter an order of possession unless the landlord has shown the tenant a proper termination notice and the court has accepted that notice into evidence. Without that notice in the record, the judge has no basis to award possession.

If you own a rented house and are thinking about selling it, this is the timeline that decides how long the tenant stays. Everything below runs on court calendars and notice periods, not on the date you decide to list.

Which notice periods apply before a landlord can file?

The notice period depends on what the tenant did, and each type has its own clock under Va. Code 55.1-1245. The table summarizes the pieces that matter most when a house is rented and you want to sell it.

SituationWhat the statute says
Unpaid rentWritten notice, then 14 days for the tenant to pay before the landlord may terminate and sue for possession
Breach that can be fixedNotice that the lease ends no sooner than 30 days after receipt unless the problem is fixed within 21 days
Breach that cannot be fixedNotice that the lease ends no sooner than 30 days after receipt
Criminal or willful act threatening health or safetyLandlord may end the lease immediately and seek possession; first hearing within 15 calendar days of service
Repeat breach of the same kind30-day notice that refers to the earlier breach
Tenant who is a family abuse victimLease does not end solely because of abuse against the tenant, if the abuser is barred by the landlord or a court order

The statute also says a fixable breach does not end the lease if the tenant fixes it before the date in the notice. For a rent default, that cure window is how a tenant who catches up can keep the home.

What changes for landlords with more than four rentals?

Starting July 1, 2027, a landlord who owns more than four rental units, or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four, must offer a payment plan before using the 14-day pay-or-quit route in certain small-balance cases. The text of 55.1-1245 on the Virginia legislature site lists the version that takes effect on that date alongside the current one.

  • The rule applies when the exact rent owed is no more than one month's rent plus contracted late charges.
  • The notice must state the exact amount and offer equal monthly installments over the shorter of six months or the time left on the lease.
  • The tenant can pay off the balance early with no penalty, and no extra late fees accrue while payments are on time.
  • The landlord only has to offer the plan once during the term of the rental agreement.
  • If the tenant neither pays nor enters the plan within 14 days, the landlord may terminate and proceed to court.

A small landlord with four or fewer units is not covered by that subsection. If you hold a single rented house, you will usually use the ordinary 14-day notice, but check your lease and ask a Virginia attorney which version applies on the day you serve it.

What happens after the judge awards possession?

After a judgment for possession, the landlord requests a writ of eviction, and the sheriff carries it out. Two statutes control the timing: 8.01-129 and 8.01-471.

  • A tenant has 10 days from judgment to appeal to circuit court, and the appeal bond must be posted and the writ tax paid within those 10 days.
  • A defendant who has been found indigent does not have to post an appeal bond.
  • If the landlord asks, the judge can order the writ to issue right away, but the sheriff may not evict before the 10-day appeal period ends.
  • The sheriff must serve notice of the date and time of eviction at least 72 hours before carrying out the writ.
  • If the tenant perfects an appeal, the sheriff returns the writ to the clerk who issued it.

A writ must issue within 180 days of the judgment for possession. Once issued, it is returnable within 30 days, and a writ not executed in that window is vacated by operation of law with no further order. No writ can issue if, after the judgment, the landlord and tenant sign a new written rental agreement.

What can a Virginia landlord collect on top of possession?

Under Va. Code 55.1-1251, ending the lease gives a landlord a claim for possession and rent, plus a separate claim for actual damages, reasonable attorney fees and the cost of serving notices and process.

Actual damages can include rent that would have come due until the lease term ends or a new tenancy begins, whichever is first, but the landlord must work to limit those damages. In a post-possession damages case, the landlord may not ask for accelerated rent through the end of the term.

A court can award possession and a money judgment in the same case, and the judgment does not have to be reduced by the security deposit first. After the tenant leaves, by choice or by writ, the deposit is credited under the deposit statute, which sets a 45-day window for an itemized statement.

These are claims the statute gives to the landlord. Whether a particular judgment or claim stays with a seller or moves with a sale depends on the contract, so have an attorney review it before closing.

How does a pending eviction affect selling a rented house?

A pending eviction does not stop a sale, but it changes what a buyer inherits. The closing is a deed transfer, and the tenant's rights do not disappear because the owner changed.

  • Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the security deposit statute and must return any deposit that is owed, whether or not it was handed over with the property.
  • A landlord cannot file or keep an unlawful detainer for a lease violation until the tenant has received the statement of tenant rights and responsibilities.
  • A hearing date, an appeal or an unexecuted writ can delay when the house is vacant, so closing dates should leave room.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners in all of these positions, including houses with tenants in place, and a conversation about the lease and any court papers is the quickest way to see what a sale would involve. We do not give legal advice, so bring the eviction file to an attorney as well.

What if the occupant is a former owner after a foreclosure sale?

If the former owner is still in a single-family home on the day of a foreclosure sale, Virginia treats that person as a tenant at sufferance. The successor owner can end that tenancy with a written notice given at least three days before the termination date, then file an unlawful detainer when the three days pass.

The former owner owes fair rental value from the date of the foreclosure until moving out, plus damages and reasonable attorney fees and court costs. This rule is in the same 8.01-126 that governs the eviction case itself.

This differs from the situation with a tenant who rented from the foreclosed owner, which follows different notice rules covered on the existing part of this page. If you are not sure which category an occupant falls into, ask the clerk of your local general district court before you file anything.

What did we leave to your local court?

Each general district court runs its own docket, filing hours and fee schedule, and some localities attach local resource sheets to the summons. We did not confirm any single county or city court's procedures from an official page, so we have left them out. Ask the clerk of the court where the rental house sits for current filing steps, fees and hearing days.

More questions about Virginia Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Virginia eviction take from notice to lockout?

There is no single number. A 14-day rent notice, a first hearing within 21 to 30 days of filing, a 10-day appeal window and a sheriff notice of at least 72 hours each add time, so the total depends on court dates and whether the tenant appeals.

Can a Virginia landlord evict without a court order?

No. Only a sheriff carrying out a writ of eviction can remove a tenant, and the writ comes after a judgment for possession in an unlawful detainer case.

How long is a writ of eviction good for in Virginia?

A writ must issue within 180 days of the judgment and is returnable within 30 days of issuance. A writ not executed in 30 days is vacated automatically.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent owed?

Often yes before the notice period ends. A rent notice gives 14 days to pay, and a fixable breach does not end the lease if it is fixed in time. After a judgment, a new written rental agreement signed with the landlord blocks the writ.

What does the sheriff have to do before an eviction?

The sheriff must serve notice of the date and time of eviction at least 72 hours before executing the writ, and cannot evict before the 10-day appeal period has run.

Who keeps the security deposit if the rental house is sold?

Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends must return any deposit that is owed to the tenant, even if the deposit never changed hands at closing.

Virginia Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Virginia rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Virginia?

A transfer on death deed is a recorded deed that names who receives a Virginia property when the owner dies, without that property passing through the owner's will. Under Article 5 of Title 64.2, an individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries effective at the transferor's death. The statute calls the owner the transferor and the person named to receive the property the designated beneficiary.

The law covers an interest in real property located in the Commonwealth. It applies to deeds made before, on or after July 1, 2013, as long as the transferor died on or after that date. It also leaves other ways of passing property untouched, so a will, a trust or a joint ownership arrangement can still be used.

The deed is called nontestamentary. In plain terms, it works as a deed that takes effect at death, which is why it needs the formalities of a deed and not the signing rules of a will.

What must a Virginia transfer on death deed contain to be valid?

A Virginia transfer on death deed has to meet seven requirements listed in Va. Code 64.2-628. Missing one of them is the most common way a deed fails, so the list is worth reading line by line.

  • It must contain the essential elements and formalities of a properly recordable deed made during life.
  • It must state that the transfer to the designated beneficiary happens at the transferor's death.
  • It must be recorded before the transferor dies, in the land records of the circuit court clerk's office where the property sits.
  • It must meet the recording rules in Chapter 6 of Title 55.1, and the clerk indexes it under the transferor's name as grantor.
  • Unless the transfer is for consideration, it is exempt from recordation tax.
  • For property held by joint owners, every joint owner must sign it.
  • It counts as a deed for the purposes of Va. Code 17.1-223.

The capacity needed to sign or revoke the deed is the same as the capacity needed to make a will. The deed also works without notice to the beneficiary, without the beneficiary accepting it, and without any payment or other consideration.

Can a Virginia transfer on death deed be changed or canceled?

Yes. A transfer on death deed is revocable even if the deed or another document says it is not, according to Va. Code 64.2-625. The owner keeps full control during life.

Revoking it takes a recorded document, and the law is specific about which kinds count. Section 64.2-630 lists four:

  • A new transfer on death deed that expressly revokes the earlier one, in whole or in part.
  • A new transfer on death deed that names a beneficiary inconsistent with the earlier deed.
  • A separate instrument of revocation that says so expressly.
  • A regular deed that conveys the property to someone else, so the owner no longer holds it at death.

The revoking document must be acknowledged after the original deed was acknowledged, and it must be recorded before the owner dies in the same circuit court land records. Tearing up or marking up a copy does nothing once the deed is recorded. Where several owners signed, one owner's revocation does not undo the others' share, and a deed made by joint owners is revoked only if every living joint owner revokes it. The statute also gives an optional revocation form at 64.2-636.

What happens to the property when the owner dies?

At the owner's death, the interest vests in the designated beneficiary under the deed, but only if that beneficiary outlives the owner. Va. Code 64.2-632 sets the rules, and a beneficiary who does not survive the owner loses the share.

Several details matter when a deed names more than one person or a family changes over time.

  • Concurrent beneficiaries take equal, undivided shares with no right of survivorship.
  • If one of several beneficiaries fails or lapses, that share moves to the others in proportion to what each holds.
  • A divorce or annulment after the deed was made revokes a transfer to the former spouse unless the deed says otherwise.
  • If the transferor was a joint owner and a co-owner survives, the property goes to the survivor, but it stays subject to the beneficiary named in the deed.

The beneficiary takes the property as it was at death, subject to every conveyance, mortgage, lien and other interest on it. The transfer is made without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise. A beneficiary may also disclaim all or part of the interest under Chapter 26 of Title 64.2.

Does the deed protect the property from the owner's creditors or change anything during life?

No. While the owner is alive, the deed does nothing to the owner's rights, and it does not shield the property from anyone. Section 64.2-631 lists what the deed does not do during the owner's life.

  • It does not affect the owner's right to sell, mortgage or otherwise deal with the property.
  • It does not affect the rights of creditors, current or future, even if they know about the deed.
  • It does not affect the owner's or the beneficiary's eligibility for any form of public assistance.
  • It does not give the beneficiary a legal or equitable interest.
  • It does not expose the property to claims against the beneficiary.

After death, the picture changes. Under 64.2-634, property that passed by the deed can be reached for the owner's creditors' claims, the costs of administering the estate, funeral expenses, and the allowances owed to a surviving spouse and children, to the extent the probate estate cannot cover them. When more than one property passes by deed, that liability is shared in proportion to their net values. A proceeding to enforce it must begin within one year after the death.

Is there a recordation tax on a Virginia transfer on death deed?

There is no recordation tax on recording a transfer on death deed or a revocation of one when no consideration passes between the parties. That exemption is in Va. Code 58.1-811(J), and the optional statutory forms print the same notice at the top.

The same section lists other no-consideration filings that can matter to families dealing with an inherited house.

DocumentRecordation tax ruleSection
Transfer on death deed or its revocationNone when no consideration passes58.1-811(J)
Deed of gift or quitclaim deed with no considerationNone, if the deed says so on its face58.1-811(D)
Deed of distribution from an estate or trust with no considerationNone, if the front page says it is a deed of distribution58.1-811(K)
Deed to trustees of a revocable trust, same grantors and beneficiariesExempt from the basic deed taxes when no consideration passes58.1-811(A)(11)

Confirm the exact filing fee and what the circuit court clerk wants on the cover page by calling the clerk for the county where the house sits. This guide does not state those local figures.

How does a transfer on death deed affect selling an inherited house?

A transfer on death deed can shorten the path to a sale, because the beneficiary can hold title after death without waiting for a court to open an estate for that house. It does not clear the house of debt, though, and the beneficiary receives it as is.

Here is what that means in practice for a seller in Virginia.

  • The beneficiary will usually need to show the recorded deed and the death record when a buyer or title company asks for proof of ownership.
  • Mortgages, liens and other interests on the property stay in place, because the beneficiary takes subject to them.
  • Because the transfer carries no warranty of title, a buyer's title company will look closely at the chain of records.
  • If the house is also exposed to estate claims under 64.2-634, a title company may want that question answered before closing.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners and beneficiaries who inherited a Virginia house and want to sell it as is, including houses with deferred repairs, tenants or unpaid taxes. If you hold a house through a transfer on death deed, call us and we will explain how an offer would work. We suggest speaking with a Virginia attorney about your title questions first.

When is a transfer on death deed the wrong tool?

It is the wrong tool when the owner wants to make the transfer certain and permanent, because the deed can always be revoked and the beneficiary has no claim during the owner's life. It is also a poor fit when the owner is concerned that the named person might die first, since the statute says a beneficiary who does not survive the owner loses the interest.

Some other points to weigh with an attorney:

  • A deed recorded after the owner's death does nothing, so timing matters.
  • A deed signed by one co-owner does not bind the others, and a joint owner's deed needs every joint owner's signature to be effective.
  • Where a will leaves real estate to be sold and names no other person, the executor has the power to sell and convey under Va. Code 64.2-521, which is a different route from a transfer on death deed.

More questions about Virginia Transfer on Death Deed

Is a Virginia transfer on death deed the same as a will?

No. A transfer on death deed is nontestamentary, which means it is a recorded deed that takes effect at death, while a will is a separate document that goes through probate. The capacity needed to sign either one is the same.

Does the beneficiary have to sign or accept the deed?

No. The deed is effective without notice to, delivery to or acceptance by the beneficiary during the owner's life, and without consideration. Virginia law allows the owner to record it without the beneficiary's involvement.

When must a Virginia transfer on death deed be recorded?

It must be recorded before the owner dies. It goes in the land records of the circuit court clerk's office in the county or city where the property sits, and the clerk indexes it under the owner's name as grantor.

Can I sell my house after I record a transfer on death deed?

Yes. During your life the deed does not affect your right to transfer or mortgage the property. Selling the house to someone else by a regular deed also revokes the earlier transfer on death deed, since you no longer own the property at death.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

The beneficiary's interest lapses, because it depends on surviving the owner. When several beneficiaries share the property, the lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to their interests.

Where does a Virginia probate case start?

A will is offered for probate in the circuit court of the county or independent city where the person who died had a known residence. If there was no known residence, the next choices are a county or city where real estate lies that the person owned or devised, then the place of death or where the person had other estate (Va. Code 64.2-443).

Virginia has 95 counties and 38 independent cities, and each one has its own circuit court clerk. A nursing home stay does not change the starting point: the place of legal residence is presumed to be the same as it was before the person became a patient.

The clerk, or a qualified deputy clerk, can admit a will to probate, appoint and qualify executors and administrators, and take their bonds, with the same effect as the court itself (Va. Code 64.2-444). Anyone interested in the probate may appeal a clerk's order to the circuit court within six months, without posting a bond, and the court then hears the matter fresh (Va. Code 64.2-445).

Who can act for the estate when there is a will, and when there is not?

With a will, the named executor acts. If the will names no executor, or the executor refuses, fails to give bond, dies, resigns or is removed, the court or clerk may grant administration with the will annexed. The first in line is a residual or substantial legatee or that person's designee. If that person does not apply within 30 days, administration can go to someone who would have been entitled to it had there been no will (Va. Code 64.2-500).

Without a will, the timing of who may apply is spelled out by statute. The table below summarizes the order in Va. Code 64.2-502.

Time since deathWho may be granted administration
First 30 daysA sole distributee, or one distributee holding written waivers from all other competent distributees
After 30 daysThe first distributee, or designee, who applies (with a hearing if several gave notice of intent during the first 30 days)
After 45 daysA nonprofit charitable organization that was conservator or guardian, after a diligent search and certified mail notice
After 60 daysA creditor or other person, after a diligent search for distributees and certified mail notice at least 30 days before applying

The clerk must be satisfied that the applicant is suitable and competent. The applicant signs under oath that he or she is not under a legal disability and has not been convicted of certain felonies involving fraud, theft or similar offenses, with an exception when the convicted person is the sole distributee.

What is the small asset affidavit, and does it help with a house?

The small asset affidavit lets successors collect certain assets without opening a full estate, but it covers personal property, not a deed to real estate. It applies when the entire personal probate estate is $75,000 or less (Va. Code 64.2-601).

The affidavit is made by all known successors on a form prepared by the Office of the Executive Secretary of the Supreme Court of Virginia. It must state:

  • that the personal probate estate does not exceed $75,000;
  • that at least 60 days have passed since the death;
  • that no application for a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere;
  • that any will was duly probated;
  • who the successors are and who is designated to receive the asset, with a fiduciary duty to safeguard and deliver it.

A house is real estate, so heirs who want to sell it usually need a personal representative or a will that gives someone the power to sell. If you are unsure which route fits your family, the circuit court clerk in the county or city can explain the paperwork the court accepts.

Can an executor sell the house?

An executor can sell real estate when the will directs that it be sold and names no one else to do the selling. In that case the executor has the power to sell and convey the property and to receive the proceeds (Va. Code 64.2-521).

If no executor qualifies, or those who qualified have died, resigned or been removed, an administrator with the will annexed holds that power, unless the will clearly says otherwise. When the will is silent about a sale, or the estate has no will, the heirs often sign the deed together, which is why a title company will want to see the court's grant of authority and the names of every heir.

What deadlines and costs come with a Virginia estate?

The personal representative must file an inventory with the commissioner of accounts within four months after the order giving authority. It lists the personal estate and all real estate over which the representative has the power of sale, with a market value placed on each item as of the date of death (Va. Code 64.2-1300). Reasonable expenses of determining those values count as costs of administration.

A probate tax applies to every will probated or grant of administration, at 10 cents for each $100 of estate value, and it does not apply to estates of $15,000 or less (Va. Code 58.1-1712).

Who gets paid first from the estate?

When estate assets cannot cover every claim, Virginia pays in a set order, and administration costs come first. Next come the family allowances, funeral expenses up to $5,000, and debts and taxes with preference under federal law. After those are medical and hospital bills of the last illness (capped at $4,000 per hospital or nursing home and $550 per person providing services or goods), then debts and taxes due the Commonwealth, certain fiduciary debts, child support arrears, and debts and taxes due localities. All other claims share what is left (Va. Code 64.2-528).

What happens to a mortgage on an inherited Virginia house?

In general, a mortgage stays with the property. Unless the will, a revocable trust or a transfer on death deed clearly says otherwise, specifically devised real property passes subject to any lien in place at the date of death, without a right to have the estate pay it off first. A general instruction in the will to pay debts does not change that (Va. Code 64.2-531).

The personal representative may send the lender written notice by certified mail, and the creditor then has until the later of one year after qualification or six months after the notice to file a claim with the commissioner of accounts. The statute also gives the representative a path to sell specifically devised property subject to a claim if the estate is not released within the time it sets.

What transfer taxes apply when the house is sold?

A deed admitted to record carries a state recordation tax of 25 cents on every $100 of the greater of the deed's consideration or the property's most recent tax assessment (Va. Code 58.1-801). A separate grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 applies to a deed for realty that was sold, and the seller pays it unless buyer and seller arrange otherwise (Va. Code 58.1-802).

The consideration must be on the first page of the deed, and the clerk certifies that the tax was paid before recording. Local recordation taxes may also apply, so ask the circuit court clerk for the current total in the county or city where the house stands.

What about unpaid property taxes on an estate house?

Real estate taxes are a lien that ranks ahead of other liens until paid, and the buyer or the trustee at a sale must see that sale proceeds go to the taxes due (Va. Code 58.1-3340). The estate should expect any back taxes to be settled at closing.

Local governing bodies set due dates, penalties and interest by ordinance. A late payment caused by the taxpayer's death or a medically determinable impairment is presumed not to be the taxpayer's fault if paid within 30 days of the due date, or within 120 days after a fiduciary qualifies, though interest keeps running (Va. Code 58.1-3916).

How does probate look across Virginia?

The same statutes apply everywhere in the Commonwealth, but the county or city handling your case sets the practical pace. Virginia has a population of about 8.88 million, and more than one-third of residents live in Northern Virginia, home to the state's largest jurisdiction, Fairfax County. The state spans the Tidewater coastal plain, the Piedmont, the Blue Ridge, the Shenandoah Valley and the southwestern Cumberland region (Wikipedia, Virginia).

More questions about Virginia Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I need probate to sell a house in Virginia?

In most cases, yes. If the house is titled only in the decedent's name, a personal representative or a will that gives power of sale is usually needed before a buyer's title company will insure the sale. A small asset affidavit covers personal property up to $75,000, not a deed.

How long do I have to inventory the estate?

Four months after the order that gives the personal representative authority. The inventory goes to the commissioner of accounts and lists real estate over which the representative holds the power of sale.

Can a creditor be appointed to run an estate?

Yes, but only after 60 days from the death, and only after a diligent search for distributees and certified mail notice sent at least 30 days before the application.

Is there a Virginia probate tax?

Yes. It is 10 cents for each $100 of estate value, and estates of $15,000 or less are exempt.

Does a mortgage have to be paid off before heirs can inherit?

Generally no. A specifically devised house passes subject to its mortgage unless the will or trust clearly directs payoff. The lender can still file a claim with the commissioner of accounts within the statutory time.

Can an heir sell the house before probate is finished?

The sale itself needs someone with authority to convey, such as a qualified personal representative. Ask the circuit court clerk what papers the court issues, and ask a Virginia attorney about your facts.

What the official sources say

  • Virginia starts Virginia taxable income with federal adjusted gross income, so capital gains are taxed as included in FAGI. (Tax Commissioner Ruling 11-48; source)
  • Virginia permits exclusion of gain on sale of a principal residence to the extent allowed for federal income tax purposes. (Tax Commissioner Ruling 11-48; source)

We buy Virginia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Virginia tax capital gains on a house sale?

Virginia has no separate capital gains tax. Gain from a sale is reported on the state income tax return alongside everything else, and it is taxed at the ordinary state income tax rates.

Those rates are set in Code of Virginia 58.1-320. For taxable years beginning in 1990 and later, the statute taxes Virginia taxable income at 2% up to $3,000, 3% from $3,000 to $5,000, 5% from $5,000 to $17,000, and 5.75% above $17,000. The Tax Commissioner ruling quoted earlier on this page explains that Virginia starts from federal adjusted gross income and follows the federal exclusion for a principal residence.

In practice that means the first question for a Virginia seller is the federal one. If the federal return excludes the gain, that same excluded amount is the starting point for the Virginia return.

ItemWhat the source saysSource
Virginia rate, first $3,0002%Code 58.1-320
Virginia rate, $3,000 to $5,0003%Code 58.1-320
Virginia rate, $5,000 to $17,0005%Code 58.1-320
Virginia rate above $17,0005.75%Code 58.1-320
Federal home sale exclusionUp to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint returnIRS Topic 701

Who qualifies for the $250,000 or $500,000 federal exclusion?

You qualify when you owned the home and lived in it as your main residence for at least 24 months of the five years before the sale. The IRS calls these the ownership test and the use test, and the two years do not have to be the same two years or consecutive.

On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both spouses must meet the use test on their own. The IRS also says you generally cannot take the exclusion if you excluded gain from another home sale in the two years before this one.

  • Own the home for at least 24 months out of the last 5 years.
  • Live in it as your main home for at least 24 months of the last 5 years.
  • Have not used the exclusion on a different home sale in the previous two years.
  • Military, Foreign Service, and intelligence community members on qualified extended duty may suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years.

IRS Publication 523, Selling Your Home, holds the full worksheets and the exceptions to the two-year rule.

What if I owned the house as a rental or an investment?

Then the home sale exclusion usually does not apply, and the gain is taxed as capital gain. A house you held for more than one year gives a long-term gain, and one you held for a year or less gives a short-term gain that is taxed as ordinary income.

For 2025, the IRS says the rate on most net capital gain is no higher than 15% for most individuals. The 0% rate applies up to $48,350 of taxable income for single filers and $96,700 for joint filers. The 15% rate runs up to $533,400 for single filers and $600,050 for joint filers, and 20% applies above those levels.

Two other federal points matter to landlords. The part of a gain that is unrecaptured section 1250 gain is taxed at a maximum rate of 25%. Higher earners may also owe the net investment income tax, which the IRS covers in Topic 559.

These federal rates stack on top of the Virginia rates above, because Virginia taxes the gain as income.

How do I figure my gain?

Gain equals the amount you realized from the sale minus your adjusted basis. Basis is generally what you paid, including purchase costs, plus improvements that add to the property's value and minus items like depreciation and insurance reimbursements for casualty losses.

Keep records of roofs, additions, kitchens, and anything else that adds to value, because they raise basis and shrink the gain. A loss on the sale of your personal home is not deductible, according to the IRS.

  • Start with the contract price and the settlement statement.
  • Add documented capital improvements to your original cost.
  • Subtract depreciation if any part of the house was a rental.
  • Compare the result with the $250,000 or $500,000 limit.

If you received the house as a gift or inheritance, your basis is not figured the usual way. The IRS points to Publication 551, Basis of Assets, for those cases, so read it before you assume a number.

Is there a form or a report when the sale closes?

Yes. If you get Form 1099-S, Proceeds From Real Estate Transactions, you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable, and you must also report it if you cannot exclude all of the gain. The IRS tells filers to use Form 8949 and Schedule D when required.

If you sell under an installment contract, where part of the price is paid in a later year, the installment method applies unless you elect out. The home sale exclusion remains available even when you defer some gain that way.

A large gain can also mean estimated tax payments, which the IRS discusses in Publication 505.

What other Virginia costs hit a seller at closing?

Two charges come up most often: the state grantor tax on the deed and any unpaid real estate tax. Neither is an income tax, but both come out of what you walk away with.

Code 58.1-802 imposes a grantor tax of 50 cents for each $500 of consideration. The seller pays it, though buyer and seller may agree to split it differently, and the clerk of court certifies it before the deed can be recorded. Half the tax goes to the state and half to the locality.

Code 58.1-3340 gives the real estate tax lien priority over any other lien. The purchaser at a sale must see that proceeds go to taxes and levies on the property, and the seller's share of tax is prorated by contract.

Cities bill on their own schedules. In Virginia Beach, for example, installments are due December 5 and June 5, and the city is an independent city with its own Treasurer.

When do inherited and rental houses change the picture?

The federal basis rule for inherited property differs from the usual cost rule. The IRS directs people who receive property by inheritance to Publication 551 for their basis, and holding-period rules for property acquired from a decedent are covered in Publication 544.

For a rental, the depreciation you claimed lowers your basis and can create the unrecaptured section 1250 gain mentioned above. A landlord who sells a house with a tenant in place may also face questions about the lease, which the Virginia eviction notice guide on this site covers.

  • Inherited house: confirm basis with Publication 551 or a tax professional before you set a price.
  • Rental house: add up depreciation taken in every year of ownership.
  • Primary home: confirm the 24-month tests before you list or accept an offer.

When does a quick as-is sale make tax sense?

It makes sense when carrying costs, repairs, or a looming tax bill would eat up more than a discounted price loses. A faster sale can limit months of mortgage, insurance, and real estate tax payments, and it gives you a firm closing date for tax planning.

The tax result itself does not depend on who the buyer is, since gain is figured from your price and basis. What a quick sale changes is timing, the number of installments you carry, and the repairs you skip.

Ask a CPA or enrolled agent to run your numbers before you accept any offer. We buy houses as-is and can share a closing timeline, but we do not give tax advice.

More questions about Virginia Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Virginia have a capital gains tax?

No separate one. Virginia taxes the gain as part of income at its ordinary rates, which top out at 5.75% on income above $17,000 under Code 58.1-320.

How much gain can I exclude when I sell my Virginia home?

Up to $250,000, or up to $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the ownership and use tests of 24 months out of the last 5 years. Virginia follows the federal exclusion, according to the ruling summarized above.

Do I report the sale if the whole gain is excluded?

You must report it if you receive Form 1099-S, even when the gain is fully excludable. You must also report it if you cannot exclude all the gain.

How long must I own a rental house for long-term capital gain treatment?

You must hold it for more than one year. A gain on property held one year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income.

Can I deduct a loss on my Virginia home sale?

Not for a personal home. The IRS says losses on the sale of personal-use property such as your home are not deductible.

Who pays the Virginia grantor tax?

The seller pays it by default, at 50 cents per $500 of consideration, but the buyer and seller may agree that the buyer pays part or all.

What the official sources say

  • Treasurer may suspend sale under an installment agreement not exceeding 72 months. (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)
  • Owner, heirs, devisees, successors and assigns may redeem before the judicial sale date by paying into court taxes, penalties, interest, costs and attorney fee. (Va. Code 58.1-3974; source)
  • A money judgment becomes a lien on real estate when recorded on the judgment lien docket. (Va. Code 8.01-458; source)
  • Anyone who paid taxes on the real estate has a lien for taxes paid plus 6 percent annual interest. (Va. Code 58.1-3974; source)

Get My Cash Offer →

How does a Virginia tax sale work?

A Virginia locality starts a tax sale by filing a lawsuit in the circuit court of the county or city where the property lies, to enforce the lien for delinquent taxes and sell the real estate (Va. Code 58.1-3967). The process follows the rules for a creditor's claim to sell real estate to enforce a judgment lien, except where a statute changes them.

Everyone with an interest must be named: lienors, anyone claiming title, and the beneficiary and trustees under a deed of trust. Title sold at the judicial sale is free of the claims of those parties, and former owners can claim surplus afterward.

When can a property be sold for delinquent taxes?

The usual trigger is taxes still delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the date they became due. For property with a condemned structure, a nuisance, a derelict building or a blighted declaration, the trigger is the first anniversary (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Real estate assessed at $100,000 or less is treated differently. On a court finding that taxes are delinquent on December 31 after the first anniversary, the property is deemed subject to sale by public auction after proper notice. The same applies to certain unpaid local lien costs for abatement or repair.

SituationEarliest sale trigger
Ordinary parcelDecember 31 after the second anniversary of the due date
Condemned, nuisance, derelict or blightedDecember 31 after the first anniversary
Assessed at $100,000 or less (court finding)December 31 after the first anniversary

In a qualifying locality with unpaid abatement costs, the periods can be shortened to six months for the condemned or blighted categories.

What notice does the owner get?

The collecting officer must send a notice at least 30 days before starting court action. It goes to the owner's last known address in the treasurer's records and to the property address if that is different and is a numbered, named street address. The notice tells the owner that a payment agreement of up to 72 months may be requested (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

The officer must also publish a list of the properties at least once in a local newspaper, at least 30 days before the case is filed. The costs of that publication, the court's reasonable attorney fees and title examination costs are added to what the owner owes, even if the owner pays before any case is filed.

Owners who move often or live out of state should keep the treasurer's records current. A notice that reaches an old address does not help anyone, and an owner served only by publication may petition for a rehearing, but only for good cause and only within 90 days after the sale is confirmed.

How can an owner stop the sale?

Pay everything owed before the sale date. The owner may redeem at any time before the sale by paying the accumulated taxes, penalties, interest, reasonable attorney fees and costs, including the pro rata cost of publication. A partial payment does not redeem the property or stop the lawsuit (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Heirs, devisees, successors and assigns have the same right to redeem, by paying into court before the sale date. Anyone who pays taxes on the property gets a lien for the amount paid, with interest at six percent a year (Va. Code 58.1-3974).

Other options in the statute:

  • The treasurer may suspend the sale under an installment agreement of up to 72 months, which must also cover current taxes as they come due.
  • A person who is not a party but claims ownership through a will or intestate succession can send written notice to the treasurer, who may suspend the case and ask the court to add that person as a party.
  • The court may refer the parties to a dispute resolution proceeding.

If the owner defaults on an installment plan, the treasurer can void it on 15 days' written notice, the case can go forward without repeating the notice, and no second plan is available for three years.

What happens to heirs when the owner has died?

Heirs have a built-in path. The statute lets an individual who claims ownership by testate or intestate succession notify the treasurer in writing, and the treasurer may suspend the action while seeking leave to add that individual as a party. If the court finds the person holds an ownership interest, that person has 30 days to enter an installment agreement for the delinquent amounts, over no more than 72 months (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

This is a place where an estate and a tax problem meet. If probate has not started, the person with the strongest claim should contact both the circuit court clerk and the treasurer quickly. Our Virginia probate guide explains who can qualify.

What are the costs of waiting?

Costs grow in three ways. Penalty and interest keep accruing under the locality's ordinance, with interest capped at 10 percent a year at first and a higher ceiling in later years. The locality may also recover attorney or collection agency fees actually contracted for, up to 20 percent of the delinquent taxes and charges (Va. Code 58.1-3916).

Real estate tax is also a lien ahead of every other lien. It stays that way until actual payment, so a buyer or a lender cannot get around it, and a sale of any kind needs the tax paid from proceeds (Va. Code 58.1-3340). The lien covers rents for the current year as well.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Virginia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What is left over after a judicial sale?

The former owner and the heirs, devisees, successors or assigns are entitled to the surplus after taxes, penalties, interest, reasonable attorney fees, costs and liens, but the burden is on the claimant to prove entitlement. If nobody claims the surplus within two years after the sale is confirmed, the clerk pays it to the locality. A governing body may grant relief by ordinance and pay over an amount it considers appropriate to a person who shows prior entitlement (Va. Code 58.1-3967).

The grantor's transfer tax of 50 cents per $500 does not apply when the grantor is a locality at a judicial sale of tax-delinquent property (Va. Code 58.1-802).

Why sell before the sale date?

A private sale lets you choose the buyer and the timing, and any tax lien is paid from proceeds, so what remains is yours. A judicial sale happens on the court's schedule, and surplus can take time and proof to claim. Equity in a house with a lien can also disappear into costs if the case grows.

Virginia has 95 counties and 38 independent cities, and each one runs its own treasurer's office and circuit court (Wikipedia, Virginia). That means the list, notices and fees depend on where the house stands. Ask the treasurer for a written payoff, ask the circuit court clerk whether a case has been filed, and compare that figure to what a buyer is offering.

More questions about Virginia Tax Sales

Can I stop a Virginia tax sale by paying part of what I owe?

No. The statute says partial payment is not enough to redeem the property and does not suspend or end the court action. Redemption requires all taxes, penalties, interest, attorney fees and costs, unless the treasurer agrees to an installment plan.

How long can a payment plan last?

Up to 72 months, and it must also keep current taxes paid as they come due. Defaulting lets the treasurer void the plan on 15 days' written notice.

Does the locality have to notify me before suing?

Yes. A notice must be sent at least 30 days before court action, to the owner's address on file and to the property address if different, and a list of properties must be published in a local newspaper.

Do heirs have any rights if the owner died?

Yes. Heirs, devisees, successors and assigns may redeem before the sale, and a person claiming through a will or intestate succession can ask the treasurer to suspend the case.

Who gets the money if the property sells for more than the taxes?

The former owner and heirs, devisees, successors or assigns, after taxes, fees, costs and liens, if they prove entitlement within two years of the sale's confirmation. After that it goes to the locality.

Can I sell my house after the lawsuit starts?

The statute lets an owner redeem any time before the sale by paying what is owed, which can be done from a sale's proceeds. Confirm payoff and timing with the treasurer and the court clerk first.
